verdicts.note: Attacked on direction: she also lists investment in housing, infrastructure and rural health care [S1][S4]. But her lead plank is a long-range plan to 'live within our means' [S3][S4], every department reporting what its spending delivers [S6], and efficiency and partnership before asking residents to pay more [S6], plus 'spending wisely, planning for rainy days' [S1]. A lean toward audit-and-restrain, not the pole: -1 medium holds. S1, S3 and S6 support the basis.

Walk-in permitting [S3][S4] and county stock building plans [S10] are supply-side and deregulatory; she proposes no public-housing, rent or tenant measure. -1 rather than -2 is right because housing is otherwise only a general goal [S1].

The basis argues mostly toward the proven-record pole while the score sits on the renewal side. On renewal: no county office, PCO only [S1], first run for countywide office. On record: she pitches inside knowledge of county budgets, financial software and grants from her time as WSU Extension's finance administrator [S3][S8], is the endorsed successor of the outgoing commissioner and four former commissioners plus a former auditor and clerk [S5], and wants decisions to rest on 'institutional memory' [S6]. She makes no outsider or generational-change pitch. That profile is genuinely mixed: 0, medium. Her opponent's +2 still marks the contrast.

The reform axis is money and power in politics (PAC money, term limits, RCV, dark money). The basis rests on governance style (collaboration, continuity, impact reporting), which is off-axis; her wish to move 'away from a personality based advocacy system' toward systems and documents [S6] is about administration, not political structure. The only on-axis evidence is an endorsement pattern within party and interest-group structures (24th LD Democrats, WEA PAC, five current and former commissioners [S5]) and a collaborative-leadership pitch [S4]. She states nothing on PAC money or structural reform. Direction holds as an indirect inference: low.

Attacked on strength: he proposes no tax cut, and 'growth pays for growth' [S4] shifts infrastructure costs to new development rather than reducing taxes. But the pamphlet names balancing the budget 'without further tax increases' the county's biggest challenge [S1], which is pole_a's 'oppose new taxes', and he backs it with possible service cuts [S1]. -2 at medium (one explicit statement, with S4 as supporting context) holds; the ESSB 6346 single-vote rule does not apply to a county candidate.

Attacked on direction: his on-demand transit and mobility-hub ideas [S3][S10] and grant-financed infrastructure districts [S4] are new programs. But the budget platform is explicit and repeated: hard decisions that 'may mean cuts in some services', 'measurable change, stronger oversight' for ineffective programs [S1], and criticism of reliance on grants and a growing administrative structure [S3]. The infrastructure districts are financed mainly by connection charges, assessments and developers [S4]. -2 high holds.

Permitting review to lower costs [S1] and a 'market-oriented public-private partnership' in which 'Developers Must Benefit' [S4] are pole_a; the 80-140% AMI targeting and resale-attached equity stake [S4] keep it short of -2. Citation gap: the basis mentions the Habitat for Humanity model, which comes from the Sept. 30 forum [S10]; S10 should be added to the citations. Score and confidence stand.

The only evidence is a passage in his 'why I am running' essay about growing up amid 'apocalyptic expectations' where 'climate fears filled the news' and the toll such narratives took on young people [S3]. That is a remark about media narratives, not a position on carbon pricing, energy costs or energy sources, which is what the axis measures. His one energy-adjacent policy points the other way: on-demand transit and mobility hubs to 'get cars off the road' [S3][S10]. No policy position either way; drop the score.

No prior elected office [S1], first run [S8], no endorsements beyond the county party's request [S8], and he runs against what he calls the county's governing philosophy [S3]. The party recruitment [S3][S8] is the only insider tie and does not give him a record. +2 medium holds as a profile description.

Off-axis. The reform axis is money and power in politics: PAC money, term limits, dark-money bans, RCV, direct democracy. The basis cites changing the county's governing philosophy, rewriting the Critical Areas Ordinance [S7] and forcing 'measurable change' in underperforming programs [S1]. Those are land-use and spending positions, already reflected on housing and spending. The dossier records nothing on campaign money or structural political reform, and his only institutional tie is that the county Republican Party recruited him [S3][S8]. Drop the score.

note: Missing scores considered and not proposed: Scalf on taxes ('grow the tax base' and 'before asking residents to pay more' [S3][S6] imply no direction), Scalf on climate (land, salmon and water protection [S3][S10] are not climate or energy policy), and safety for both (wildfire and emergency preparedness only [S4][S6]). Display review: office_does matches contest S2 and S6. race_blurb: one wording point. 'Commissioner Greg Brotherton is retiring' goes beyond the dossier, which says only that he is not seeking re-election (contest S2); suggested: 'Open seat: Commissioner Greg Brotherton is not seeking re-election.' The rest of the blurb is accurate: Kler and Austin are the two other former District 3 commissioners among her endorsers (Scalf S5), and the primary order and percentages match contest S4. Summaries and all ten highlights match the cited sources (Scalf S1, S3-S8, S10, S11; Nieman S1, S3, S4, S7, S8, S10, S11). Nieman's 'Critical Areas Ordinance loosened' is a fair short form of the buffer-flexibility and threshold proposals on his CAO page [S7].
